title: The arahant ideal
hookLine: Theravada honors the arahant, fully freed, who also teaches and helps

cards: A young mother loses everything in one terrible stretch: her children, her husband, her parents. The old commentaries tell how she wandered so lost in grief that her clothes fell away and people drove her off.
You may remember her from year one: Patacara. She came to the Buddha, he spoke to her, and over time, the texts say, her mind was freed. Then she taught.
The verses of the early nuns, the Therigatha, remember women who came to her in their own grief and found their way. A woman freed, who turned around and helped.

teach.h: ARAHANT: ONE WHO HAS FINISHED THE PATH.
teach.b: First, the word. In Pali, arahant names one who has finished the path: greed, hatred and delusion are gone, and there is no more becoming.
In the Theravada it's the goal of practice, for monks and nuns, and in some stories for lay people too. The Buddha himself is called an arahant in the old chant of praise. Second, what it feels like.

teach.h: NO SUFFERING FOR ONE WHO HAS FINISHED.
teach.b: The Dhammapada has a whole chapter on the arahant, and in Max Müller's translation it opens: "There is no suffering for him who has finished his journey, and abandoned grief, who has freed himself on all sides, and thrown off all fetters."
Third, the turning back. The arahant is not a hermit who closes the door.

teach.h: SENT OUT FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.
teach.b: In the Vinaya, the Buddha sends his first freed disciples out on the roads, in the Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translation, "for the gain of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world."
Sariputta taught. Patacara taught. In Theravada lands, people still seek out teachers they regard as freed, for a word, a blessing, a way through.
In Chinese temples, halls of arhat statues, the luohan, line the walls: laughing, scratching, sleeping, thinking, each one a freed disciple.
The Theravada puts the arahant at the center; other schools honor arahants too, in their own way. Tomorrow, a second ideal.

how: In Theravada Buddhism the arahant is the goal of the path, and devotees honor the Buddha and his freed disciples with chanting, bows and visits to respected teachers; some Chinese temples keep halls of luohan statues.

games.q: you are Patacara. your mind is freed at last, and grieving women begin to seek you out. what do you do?
o: withdraw into silence; the work is done.
teach them the way you found.
send them all to the Buddha instead.
games.why: she taught. the Therigatha remembers women who came to her in grief and found their way.

practice: Bring to mind one freed teacher: Patacara, Sariputta, or someone in your own life who seemed to carry very little and gave freely anyway.
Picture their face, a word they said, the way they listened, and let gratitude rise if it comes. If you bow, a small nod of the head is enough.

wordCard.voice: The arahant ideal. One who has finished the path, fully freed from greed, hatred and delusion, and who, in the texts, turns back to teach. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali arahant (Sanskrit arhat): one who has finished the path, fully freed.

carryVoice: Your line: fully freed. Freed, and still turning back to help. Until tomorrow.
